title: Low-Dimensional Adaptation of Rectified Flow: A Diffusion and Stochastic Localization Perspective
claim: A deterministic sampler leaves many endpoints in low-density regions; adding a stochastic score-driven correction acts as a guardrail and reduces them.
layout: 2 side-by-side scatter panels, left-to-right, shared axes, yellow loops and purple arrows
description: Two side-by-side 2-D scatter panels share axes running from -10 to 10 in y and 0 to 20 in x. Panel (a) is titled Deterministic (RF) and panel (b) is titled Stochastic (STOC-RF). In each panel a gray Gaussian blob of initial samples at the origin sends thin gray trajectory lines to two target modes. One mode is a round blue contour with teal generated samples in the upper right. The other is an elongated diagonal blue contour in the lower middle. Orange dots mark low-density endpoints, and yellow loops circle them. In (a) the trajectories are straight and many orange endpoints sit outside the contours. In (b) the trajectories are wiggly, purple arrows labeled Score-driven correction (schematic) point toward the modes, and fewer orange endpoints appear. A legend at the bottom explains target density, initial samples, generated samples and low-density endpoints. The eye goes first to the orange dots circled in yellow.
caption: Trajectories and generated samples from deterministic (RF) and stochastic (STOC-RF) samplers targeting a two-component Gaussian mixture. \blue{Blue} contours indicate target density, and highlighted endpoints lie in low-density regions. {\color{violet}Purple} arrows illustrate the score-driven component of the Langevin correction, which locally directs samples toward higher density and can counteract accumulated sampling errors—acting as a soft “guardrail.” The stochastic sampler exhibits fewer low-density endpoints in this example.
abstract: In recent years, Rectified flow (RF) has gained considerable popularity largely due to its generation efficiency and state-of-the-art performance. In this paper, we investigate how well RF automatically adapts to the intrinsic low dimensionality of the support of the target distribution to accelerate sampling. We show that, using a carefully designed end-point adapted time-discretization scheme and with sufficiently accurate drift estimates, the RF sampler enjoys an iteration complexity of order $O(k/\varepsilon)$ (up to log factors), where $\varepsilon$ is the precision in total variation distance and $k$ is the intrinsic dimension of the target distribution. In addition, we show that the denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) procedure is equivalent to a stochastic version of RF by establishing a novel connection between these processes and stochastic localization. Building on this connection, we further design a stochastic RF sampler that also adapts to the low-dimensionality of the target distribution under mild requirements on the accuracy of the drift estimates, and also with a specific time schedule. We illustrate the efficacy of newly designed time-discretization schedules with simulations on the synthetic data and text-to-image (T2I) data experiments.
